Question no. 1. Distinguish between Insolvency and Bankruptcy?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The term insolvency and bankruptcy are the frequently used terms under the IBC, 2016.  
Insolvency is used for both individuals and organizations. It signifies a situation of  
financial distress where the debtor's liabilities exceed their assets, and they are unable  
to meet their financial obligations. For individuals, it is known as bankruptcy and for  
corporate it is called corporate insolvency. Under the IBC Insolvency is regarded as a  
“state” where assets are insufficient to meet the liabilities. If untreated, insolvency will  
lead to bankruptcy for non-corporate and liquidation of corporate. Bankruptcy, on the  
other hand, is a legal proceeding involving a person or business that is unable to repay  
outstanding debts or is a legal process that arises from insolvency.  
There are some differences between both insolvency and bankruptcy are:  
 Meaning:  


Insolvency relates to the financial state of being unable to pay debts.  
Bankruptcy refers to the formal legal process that follows insolvency.  
 Nature:  


Insolvency is temporary and amount can be recoverable. It is a state of  
economic distress.  
Bankruptcy is permanent and final declaration of insolvency by the  
authorities. It is the conclusion.  
 Process:  


Insolvency is involuntary.  
Bankruptcy is voluntary.  
 Arises when:  


Insolvency arises when assets are not sufficient to pay off liabilities.  
Untreated insolvency results in bankruptcy in the case of individuals and  
liquidation in the case of corporates.  
Thus, insolvency signifies financial distress, while bankruptcy is the formal legal  
process that addresses the insolvency situation through the distribution of assets  
among creditors. The IBC provides a comprehensive framework to deal with both  
insolvency and bankruptcy situations, aiming to achieve a fair and efficient resolution.

Question no. 2. Who may initiate the corporate insolvency resolution process under the under  
IBC?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
IBC provides a structured framework for the initiation of the Corporate Insolvency  
Resolution Process (“CIRP”), ensuring that the process is triggered by relevant parties  
and under specific circumstances of default. The initiation of the CIRP is a significant  
step in resolving insolvency situations, and the involvement of different stakeholders  
ensures a balanced approach to the process.  
Section 6 of the IBC provides the list of persons who may initiate corporate insolvency  
resolution process, where any corporate debtor commits a default, they may initiate  
corporate insolvency resolution process in respect of such corporate debtor. The following  
can initiate CIRP as per IBC:  
 Financial Creditor (section 7): A financial creditor, which includes banks, financial  
institutions, and other entities that have extended financial debt to the corporate  
debtor, can initiate the CIRP.  
 Operational Creditor (section 8 & 9): An operational creditor, which includes  
suppliers of goods and services to the corporate debtor, can also initiate the CIRP.  
They need to issue a demand notice to the corporate debtor for the unpaid  
operational debt, and if the debt is not paid or resolved within the stipulated time,  
they can approach the Authority to initiate the process.  
 Corporate Applicant (section 10): A corporate debtor itself/applicant can initiate  
the CIRP which allows the corporate debtor to take control of its financial distress  
and propose a plan for its resolution.  
Thus, the initiation of the CIRP leads either to a revival of corporate debtors or the  
liquidation is called for in case revival is not possible.

Question no. 3. What is time limit within which the CIRP should be completed as per the IBC?  
Ans:  
.
Introduction:  
As per the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (“IBC”), the Corporate Insolvency  
Resolution Process (“CIRP”) should ideally be completed within a time frame of 180 days  
as per section 12(1) of the IBC. This period begins from the date of admission of the  
application by the Adjudicating Authority i.e., NCLT to initiate such process.  
However, this initial time limit of 180 days can be extended by the NCLT by an additional  
period of 90 days if the CIRP process has not been completed within the initial days and  
for valid reasons. Therefore, the maximum permissible time for completing the CIRP is  
270 days in case of grant of extension. However, any extension of the period of the  
corporate insolvency resolution process shall not be granted more than once. The  
maximum time within which CIRP has to be mandatorily completed, including any  
extension or litigation period, is 330 days.  
It's important to note that timely completion of the CIRP is a critical aspect of the IBC, as  
it aims to ensure efficient resolution of insolvency cases, protect the interests of  
stakeholders, and maintain the viability of the corporate debtor. Extending the time frame  
beyond the prescribed limits requires approval from the NCLT, and the process must be  
diligently managed to avoid unnecessary delays and ensure the best possible outcome  
for all parties involved.

Question no. 4. How is an Interim Resolution Professional appointed in a CIRP?  
Ans:  
.
Introduction:  
Insolvency resolution professional and resolution professional are the key professionals  
and pillar under the Insolvency and bankruptcy code, 2016. These professionals are the  
whole and sole of the company after the insolvency application is approved by the  
Adjudicating Authority. Section 16 of the IBC provides that the Adjudicating Authority  
shall appoint an interim resolution professional on the insolvency commencement  
date.  
Where the application for corporate insolvency resolution process is made by a financial  
creditor or the corporate debtor, as the case may be, the resolution professional, as  
proposed respectively in the application under section 7 or section 10, shall be appointed  
as the interim resolution professional if no disciplinary proceedings are pending against  
him. However, where the application for corporate insolvency resolution process is made  
by an operational creditor and  

no proposal for an interim resolution professional is made, the Adjudicating  
Authority shall make a reference to the Board for the recommendation of an  
insolvency professional who may act as an interim resolution professional;  
a proposal for an interim resolution professional is made the operational creditor,  
the resolution professional as proposed, shall be appointed as the interim  
resolution professional, if no disciplinary proceedings are pending against him.  

When a reference is made to the Board by the Adjudicating Authority as mentioned above,  
it shall, within ten days of the receipt of a reference from the Adjudicating Authority,  
recommend the name of an insolvency professional who shall act as the interim  
resolution professional. The term of the interim resolution professional shall  
continue till the date of appointment of the resolution professional under section 22 of the  
IBC.  
The role of the Interim Resolution Professional is crucial in initiating and facilitating  
the early stages of the CIRP. They ensure the preservation of the corporate debtor's  
assets, verify creditor claims, and lay the groundwork for the subsequent phases of the  
resolution process. In other words, the IRP's role is to take control and manage the affairs  
of the corporate debtor during the initial phase of the CIRP.

Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016??

2016, what is the mechanism by which an Interim Resolution Professional is designated?

Question no. 5. What does moratorium mean under IBC. Explain its objective under the purview  
of the IBC?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The term “Moratorium” is nowhere defined in the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.  
However, moratorium in terms of IBC means a period wherein no judicial proceedings  
for recovery, enforcement of security interest, sale or transfer of assets, or termination of  
essential contracts can be instituted or continued against the Corporate Debtor. The  
Adjudicating Authority while admitting an application against the corporate debtor  
is required to declare the moratorium period under Section 14 of the IBC. The main  
purpose of declaring the moratorium period is to keep the Corporate Debtor’s assets  
intact during the CIRP. In other words, it provides a breathing space to the corporate  
debtor and its assets to allow the insolvency resolution process to take place without  
external disruptions.  
As per the provisions of the IBC when an order declaring a moratorium is issued, it  
prohibits the institution of new litigation or the continuation of existing suits or procedures  
against the corporate debtor, including the execution of any judgement, decision, or order.  
It creates a calm period or as mentioned above a breathing space for the corporate  
debtor which guarantees that the already economically challenged corporate debtor  
maximizes its asset realization and thus, achieves a rapid resolution. As the very  
objective of declaring moratorium is to retain the corporate debtor’s assets together  
throughout the insolvency proceedings, enabling the organized finalization of the  
procedures envisioned throughout the insolvency proceedings, and making sure that the  
corporate debtor can resume as a viable business. Thus, it protects corporate debtor  
not only from new recovery claims during the insolvency resolution process but also from  
current claims that may be pending before multiple authorities.  
As per the IBC moratorium begins from the date of admission of the insolvency  
application by the Adjudicating Authority and remains in effect until the completion of  
the insolvency resolution process. This ensures that the resolution process takes place  
without unnecessary delays and external disturbances. Further, if the Adjudicating  
Authority approves the resolution plan or passes an order for liquidation of corporate  
debtor, the moratorium ceases to have effect from the date of such approval of resolution  
plan or liquidation order, as the case may be.  
Thus, we can say that the concept of moratorium aims to maintain the status quo and  
prevent any further erosion of the corporate debtor's assets during the resolution  
process. It provides a temporary shield to the corporate debtor from aggressive recovery  
actions, allowing the insolvency resolution process to proceed in an orderly and efficient  
manner.  
6
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes

Question no. 6. Explain the process and conditions for initiating voluntary liquidation by a  
corporate debtor under IBC?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
A corporate person who intends to liquidate itself voluntarily and has either not  
committed any default, has no debt or in case of having debt, it will be able to pay  
its debts in full; from the proceeds of assets to be sold in the liquidation, may initiate  
voluntary liquidation process as per section 59 of the IBC, 2016 (“Code”)  
Under section 59(3) of the Code a corporate person may initiate the voluntary liquidation  
process after fulfilling the following conditions:  
 Declaration of Solvency stating that:  

the corporate person has no debt or that it will be able to pay its debts in  
full; from the proceeds of assets and  

the corporate person is not being liquidated to defraud any person;  
 Declaration be accompanied with:  

Audited financial statements and record of business operations previous  
two years or for the period since its incorporation, whichever is later;  

Report of the valuation of the assets of the company  
 Within four weeks of a declaration:  

special resolution requiring the corporate person to be liquidated  
voluntarily and appointing an insolvency professional to act as the  
liquidator; or  

resolution to voluntarily liquidate as a result of expiry of the period of its  
duration, if any, fixed by its Articles or occurrence of any event for which  
the Articles provide that the company be dissolved, & appointment of an  
insolvency professional to act as the liquidator.  
 If corporate person owes any debt, creditors representing two-thirds in value of the  
debt of the corporate person shall approve the aforesaid resolution, within seven  
days of such resolution.  
7
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes  
 RoC & Board to be notified about the resolution within 7 days of such resolution  
or the subsequent approval by the creditors, as the case may be.  
Once the approval of the creditors is taken, the voluntary liquidation process in respect of  
a corporate person shall be deemed to have commenced from the date of passing of  
the resolution.  
 Process for the voluntary liquidation:  
 Public Announcement  
 Submission and verification of claims  
 Realization of assets by the liquidator  
 Distribution of assets  
 Filing of Report to RoC & NCLT  
 Once the affairs of the Corporate Person have been completely wound up and its  
assets are fully liquidated, then the Liquidator shall make an application to the  
NCLT for dissolution.  
 Once the NCLT passes an order for Dissolution, the Corporate Person shall stand  
dissolved.  
Thus, voluntary liquidation under IBC occurs when all the company’s board members  
mutually agree not to continue the business and dissolve the company of its assets  
and pay off the debts.

Question no. 7. Describe the composition, powers, and functions of the National Company Law  
Tribunal as the principal adjudicating authority under IBC?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The National Company Law Tribunal (“NCLT/Tribunal”) is a quasi-judicial organization  
which serves as the principal adjudicating authority for matters related to insolvency  
and bankruptcy. It is the successor entity to the Company Law Board and and Board for  
Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR). It was established based on the  
recommendations of the Justice Erandi Committee with the primary objective to  
consolidate and streamline the adjudication process of corporate disputes and insolvency  
8
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes  
proceedings. Under Section 408 of the Companies Act, 2013 the Central Government  
constitutes the National Company Law Tribunal.  
NCLT consists of a Principal Bench in New Delhi and several Regional Benches located  
across different states in India. It consists of a President and such number of Judicial  
and Technical members, as the Central Government may deem necessary, to be  
appointed. The Tribunal plays a very important role as the adjudicating authority under the  
IBC, 2016. The powers and functions of the Tribunal as the principal adjudicating  
authority under IBC are:  
 Adjudication of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process  
 Approval of Resolution Plans  
 Liquidation Orders  
 Insolvency-related Disputes are adjudicated and resolved by it, including those  
arising from the CIRP process, claims of creditors, and challenges to resolution  
plans.  
NCLT as a specialized forum expedites the resolution process, maintains transparency,  
and ensures the protection of the rights of stakeholders involved in insolvency and  
bankruptcy cases. It facilitates the timely revival of viable businesses and the efficient  
realization of assets, contributing to the IBC's fundamental goal of resolving distress  
situations in a structured and equitable manner.

Question no. 8. What is a Committee of Creditors (“CoC”) under IBC. Explain its  
constitution and the role played by it as per the provisions of IBC.  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The Committee of Creditors (“CoC”) is a pivotal entity within the Insolvency and  
Bankruptcy Code (“IBC”) framework that plays a crucial role in the corporate insolvency  
resolution process (“CIRP”). It comprises financial creditors of the corporate debtor and  
holds significant decision-making authority during the resolution proceedings. The IBC a  
“creditor-in-control” model under the Code which provides that the management of the  
corporate debtor’s affairs shall vest absolutely with the creditors in the event of financial  
distress. The CoC is the supreme decision-making body in a CIRP as the decisions  
regarding the administration of the corporate debtor are taken at the meetings of the  
Committee, based on a majority vote of the members.  
9
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes  
The constitution of the COC is as per section 18 and Section 21 of the IBC, which  
obligates the Interim Resolution Professional to constitute the CoCs, after the  
collation of the claims. As per Section 21(2) of the IBC, the Committee shall comprise  
“all financial creditors of the corporate debtor”. In other words, the CoC is composed of  
all financial creditors of the corporate debtor, including banks, financial institutions, and  
other entities holding financial claims. Each creditor shall vote in accordance with the  
voting share assigned to him based on the financial debts owed to such creditor and the  
resolution professional shall determine the voting share to be assigned to each creditor in  
the manner specified by the Board. However, a financial creditor who is a related party  
to the corporate debtor is not included in the committee of creditors and therefore, shall  
not have any voting share in the committee. In a case, where the corporate debtor owes  
financial debts to two or more financial creditors as part of a consortium or agreement,  
each such financial creditor shall be part of the committee of creditors and their voting  
share shall be determined on the basis of the financial debts owed to them.  
Operational creditors are not part of the CoC but can participate in certain discussions  
without voting rights. However, where the corporate debtor does not have financial  
creditors or where all financial creditors are its related parties, the committee of  
creditors shall comprise of operational creditors consisting of:  
 eighteen largest operational creditors by value or all operational creditors, where  
they are less than eighteen in number;  
 one representative elected by workmen; and  
 one representative elected by all employees.  
The CoC has been vested with certain crucial powers and functions under the IBC as  
under:  
 Decision-Making Authority: The CoC has the authority to make critical decisions  
during the CIRP. Major decisions, such as the appointment of a Resolution  
Professional or the approval of a resolution plan, require the CoC's approval by a  
vote of at least 66% of the voting share.  
 Appointment of RP: The CoC appoints the RP to take over the management of  
the corporate debtor and execute the insolvency resolution process. The RP acts  
as the bridge between the CoC and the corporate debtor.  
 Evaluation of Resolution Plans: The CoC evaluates and approves or rejects  
resolution plans submitted by potential resolution applicants. The resolution plan  
approved by the CoC is then presented to the Adjudicating Authority for final  
approval.  
 Protection of Interests: The CoC's decisions must consider the best interests of  
all stakeholders, including employees, shareholders, and creditors. It aims to  
maximize the value of assets and secure a viable resolution for the corporate  
debtor.  
 Negotiations and Discussions: The CoC facilitates negotiations with potential  
resolution applicants and may engage in discussions to modify or improve  
resolution plans to achieve the best possible outcome.  
10  
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes  
 Monitoring Resolution Professional's (“RP”) Activities: The CoC monitors the  
activities of the RP, ensuring transparency, accountability, and adherence to the  
resolution plan.  
 Liquidation Decision: If a viable resolution plan is not approved by the CoC within  
the stipulated timeframe, or if the approved plan fails during implementation, the  
CoC takes a decision relating to the initiation of the liquidation of the corporate  
debtor.  
Thus, the Co) serves as the driving force behind the corporate insolvency  
resolution process under the IBC. Its composition of financial creditors and  
decision-making authority ensures a collaborative and comprehensive  
approach to achieving successful insolvency resolution while safeguarding the  
interests of all stakeholders involved.

Question no. 9. Explain the entire process of CIRP as per IBC 2016.  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (“CIRP”) is a structured framework under  
the IBC, 2016, aimed at resolving the financial distress of insolvent corporate debtors. The  
process involves various stages and stakeholders, all working towards the successful  
resolution of the corporate debtor's financial issues.  
The entire CIRP process as per the IBC is a three-stage process which includes:  
 Pre-admission process section 3-11  
 Post-admission process section 12 to 32A  
 Liquidation stage section 33 to 42 and section 52 to 54  

Initiation of CIRP: It can be initiated by the corporate debtor itself, financial  
creditors, or operational creditors. They file an application before the  
Adjudicating Authority, outlining the default in payment of debt. This  
basically results in either the revival of the corporate debtor, or its  
liquidation.  
11  
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes  

Admission by the Adjudicating Authority: Upon receiving the  
application, the Adjudicating Authority examines it to ascertain if the default  
exists and if it is satisfied with the application's validity, it admits the  
application and commences the CIRP. If it rejects the application the same  
is intimated to the applicant.  

Appointment of Interim Resolution Professional: The Adjudicating  
Authority appoints an Interim Resolution Professional who takes control of  
the corporate debtor's operations and management during the initial phase.  
Moratorium Period: Upon the appointment of the IRP, a moratorium  
period begins.  
Formation of Committee of Creditors by the interim resolution  
professional consisting of financial creditors.  
Submission of Claims and Verification: The interim resolution  
professional invites claim from all creditors and verifies them.  
Appointment of Resolution Professional by the CoC from the pool of  
insolvency professionals. The RP takes over the management of the  
corporate debtor from the interim resolution professional.  
Preparation of Information Memorandum by the resolution professional  
containing details of the corporate debtor's financial position, assets, and  
liabilities.  
Invitation of Resolution Plans by the resolution professional from  
potential resolution applicants which outlines how they intend to resolve the  
financial distress of the corporate debtor.  
Evaluation and Approval of Resolution Plans by the CoC and selects  
the one that maximizes the value of assets and offers the best outcome for  
stakeholders. The approved plan is then submitted to the Adjudicating  
Authority for final approval.  









Implementation, monitoring and compliance of the Resolution Plan  
by the resolution professional.  
Conclusion of CIRP: Upon successful implementation of the resolution  
plan, the CIRP concludes, and the corporate debtor's financial distress is  
resolved. If the plan fails, liquidation of the corporate debtor may be  
initiated.  
Thus, the entire CIRP process is designed to ensure a transparent and effective  
resolution of the corporate debtor's financial issues while safeguarding the  
interests of creditors, stakeholders, and the overall economy.  
NOTE: In the initiation process you should have an idea of the documents which each  
applicant has to furnish along with the application as provided under their respective  
sections i.e., 7, 8, 9 & 10.  
12  
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes

Question no. 10. Elaborate ‘Waterfall Arrangement’ under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy  
Code, 2016.  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The 'Waterfall Arrangement' under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 refers to  
the priority order in which the proceeds from the liquidation of a corporate debtor's  
assets are distributed among various stakeholders. It outlines the sequence in which  
different classes of creditors and claimants are entitled to receive their dues from the sale  
of the corporate debtor's assets during the liquidation process.  
Section 53 of the IBC provides for a waterfall mechanism which gives a detail of the  
order and priority of the distribution of the assets of the corporate debtor among its  
stakeholders in the order of priority. As per this section the proceeds from the sale of the  
liquidation assets are distributed in the following order of priority:  
 Insolvency Resolution and Liquidation Cost  
 Secured Creditors (in case he has relinquished security interest) + Workmen’s  
Dues (for period of 24 months preceding liquidation commencement date)  
 Wages and unpaid dues to employees (other than workmen) for a period of 12  
months preceding liquidation commencement date  
 Unsecured Creditors  
 Government Dues + Secured Creditors for an unrealized amount for enforcing  
security interest  
 Any remaining debts or dues  
 Preference Shareholders, if any  
 Equity Shareholders or partners, as the case maybe  
It is important to note that each class of creditors or claimants must be paid in full before  
the next class receives any payment. The Waterfall Arrangement aims to ensure a fair  
13  
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes  
and orderly distribution of assets during the liquidation process, safeguarding the interests  
of various stakeholders while maintaining a predetermined hierarchy of payment priority.

Question no. 11. Explain the entire liquidation process under IBC 2016 in detail?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
Liquidation of a corporate debtor refers to the end of its operations or existence or the  
closing down the business of the corporate debtor. The process of liquidation can be  
initiated if the corporate debtor becomes incapable of repaying the debts or amounts owed  
by it and thus, it is the final stage of the insolvency resolution process. It is initiated when  
the efforts to revive the corporate debtor have failed, or when the resolution plan is  
not approved. The liquidation process aims to realize the maximum value from the sale  
of the corporate debtor's assets and distribute the proceeds among creditors and  
stakeholders as per the Waterfall Arrangement.  
Section 33 of the IBC provides for the initiation of the liquidation process in the  
following circumstances:  
 If the Adjudicating Authority does not receive a resolution plan for the  
corporate debtor before the expiry of the maximum time period  
 If the Adjudicating Authority rejects the resolution plan due to non-  
compliance with the requirements specified under section 31 of IBC.  
 If the resolution professional, before the confirmation of the resolution plan, informs  
the Adjudicating Authority that the committee of creditors has decided to  
liquidate the corporate debtor by at least sixty-six percent of the voting share  
 If the corporate debtor contravenes the resolution plan approved by the  
Adjudicating Authority  
The various steps involved in the liquidation of the corporate debtor are:  
 Appointment of liquidator: Once the liquidation has been initiated, a liquidator  
will be appointed to carry out the liquidation process and manage the other affairs  
of the corporate debtor. Once appointed the liquidator shall verify the claims,  
evaluate the assets, carry on the business of the corporate debtor, taking into his  
custody the assets of the corporate debtor, etc.  
14  
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes  
 Public announcement by the liquidator: The liquidator shall, after his  
appointment, issue a public announcement calling upon the creditors to submit  
their claims in relation to the corporate debtor.  
 Consolidation and verification of claims: The creditors of the corporate debtor  
will submit their claims within thirty days from the initiation of the liquidation  
process. After the receipt of the claims, the liquidator shall verify those claims.  
 Admission, rejection, and determination of the valuation of claims: Liquidator  
shall either admit or reject the claims on the basis of verification of the claims. In  
either of the case the liquidator shall communicate the same to the creditor as well  
as the corporate debtor within seven days from such decision. After all the required  
claims have been admitted by the liquidator, he shall determine the value of the  
claims for the purpose of distribution of the assets of the corporate debtor.  
 Time limit for liquidation proceedings: The liquidation proceedings should be  
completed within a period of year from the date of initiation of liquidation as per  
Regulation 44 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Liquidation  
Process) Regulations, 2016  
 Dissolution of the corporate debtor: Adjudicating Authority on the application of  
the liquidator, after the distribution of assets of the corporate debtor as per the  
priority of claims, shall dissolve the corporate debtor.  
 Appeal against the liquidator: Section 42 of the IBC provides that a creditor who  
is aggrieved by the decision of the liquidator may file an appeal to the Adjudicating  
Authority within fourteen days of the communication of such decision to the  
creditor.  
The liquidation process aims to ensure an orderly and efficient realization of assets,  
equitable distribution of proceeds, and an orderly exit for the corporate debtor from  
the market.

Question no. 12. Explain the difference, if any, between the corporate insolvency  
resolution process and the pre-packaged insolvency resolution process under the IBC,  
2016?  
15  
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The CIRP and the PPIRP are the two ways of insolvency resolution mechanism for  
resolving insolvency of the corporate debtor under the IBC, 2016. While CIRP  
provides a formal initiation of insolvency proceedings against a financially distressed  
corporate debtor to identify a viable resolution plan that maximizes the value of the  
company's assets and settles creditors' claims. The PPIRP is a relatively new  
framework introduced to streamline the insolvency resolution process which  
involves a pre-negotiated and consensual resolution plan that is agreed upon before  
formally initiating insolvency proceedings before the Authority.  
Even though both these processes aim at the insolvency resolution of the corporate debtor  
they have some noticeable differences between them as under:  
 Who can Initiate: CIRP by Corporate Debtor, Financial Creditor & Operational  
Creditor whereas PPIRP by the Corporate Debtor only  
 Against whom it can be initiated: CIRP can be initiated against the corporate  
debtor as defined under section 3(8) of the IBC whereas the PPIRP can be initiated  
against the corporate debtor classified as a micro, small or medium enterprise  
 Value of Default for filing of Application: CIRP one crore while for PPIRP ten  
lakhs  
 Time Limit for Completion: CIRP 180+90 days, (mandatorily in 330 in special  
cases) while PPIRP in 120 days  
 Base Resolution Plan: In CIRP no such requirement whereas in PPIRP  
Corporate Debtor must present it to the financial creditors before the initiation of  
the process  
 Management of the affairs of the Corporate Debtor: In CIRP Resolution  
Professional handles and manages while in PPIRP the existing management  
 Timeline for submission of Resolution Plan: In CIRP no such timeline although  
insolvency resolution process needs to be completed within 180 days whereas in  
PPIRP Resolution Professional shall submit a resolution plan after approval from  
Committee of Creditors to the Adjudicating Authority within 90 days  
 Interim period/cooling off period: 12 months between two CIRPs while in PPIRP  
three years between 2 PPIRPs  
Thus, the core difference between CIRP and PPIRP lies in the timing and approach to  
negotiations. CIRP is initiated formally and involves negotiations during the process,  
while PPIRP emphasizes pre-negotiation and consensus before the formal  
commencement of insolvency proceedings before the Authority.

insolvency resolution process as outlined in the IBC, 2016?

packaged insolvency resolution process according to the IBC, 2016?

Question no. 13. What is pre-packaged insolvency resolution process under the IBC, 2016.  
Explain the key aspects of the PPIRP.  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
PPIRP stands for "Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process," a mechanism  
introduced by the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2021. Thus, pre-packaged insolvency  
resolution process is applicable to the corporate persons classified as micro, small  
and medium enterprises. It has been introduced and made effective from 4th April 2021  
by insertion of Chapter III-A [sections 54A to 54P] being introduced in Part II of IBC.  
It is designed to facilitate a faster and more efficient resolution of stressed companies  
by allowing creditors and promoters to agree on a resolution plan before initiating the  
formal insolvency proceedings.  
PPIRP has emerged as an innovative corporate rescue method that incorporates the  
virtues of both informal i.e., out-of-court and formal i.e., judicial insolvency  
proceedings. Therefore, it is considered as s hybrid framework, as it resolves the financial  
stress of a corporate debtor as a going concern, with minimum assistance of Government.  
In other words, it is a hybrid framework as it empowers stakeholders to resolve the stress  
of a corporate debtor as a going concern, with the minimum assistance of the Government.  
It is considered fast, cost efficient, and effective in resolution of stress, much before value  
deteriorates, with the least business disruptions and without attracting the stigma attached  
with the formal insolvency process. It starts with an informal understanding, engages the  
stakeholders in between, and ends with a judicial intervention.  
The pre-requisites for initiation of PPIRP are:  
 An application for initiating pre-packaged insolvency resolution process may be  
made in respect of a corporate debtor, who commits a default as per section 4  
of at least Rs. 10 lakhs;  
 Corporate debtor has not undergone pre-packaged insolvency resolution  
process or completed corporate insolvency resolution process, as the case  
may be, during the period of three years preceding the initiation date;  
 Corporate debtor is not undergoing a corporate insolvency resolution  
process;  
 No order requiring corporate debtor to be liquidated is passed under section  
33;  
 Corporate debtor is eligible to submit a resolution plan under section 29A;  
 Financial creditors of the corporate debtor, not being its related parties, and  
representing not less than 66% in value of the financial debt due have proposed  
17  
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes  
and approved the name of the insolvency professional to be appointed as  
resolution professional for conducting the PPIRP  
 The majority of the directors or partners of the corporate debtor, as the case may  
be, have made a declaration, that:  

the corporate debtor shall file an application for initiating pre-packaged  
insolvency resolution process within a definite time period not exceeding  
ninety days;  


the pre-packaged insolvency resolution process is not being initiated to  
defraud any person; and  
the name of the insolvency professional proposed and approved to be  
appointed as resolution professional;  
 The members of the corporate debtor have passed a special resolution, or at  
least 3/4th of the total number of partners, as the case may be, of the corporate  
debtor have passed a resolution, approving the filing of an application for initiating  
pre-packaged insolvency resolution process.  
The PPIRP streamlines the insolvency resolution process for the MSMEs by enabling a  
pre-negotiated agreement between the corporate debtor and its financial creditors. This  
approach enhances efficiency, encourages collaboration, and aims to achieve a smoother  
and faster resolution while adhering to the provisions of the IBC, 2016.

Question no. 14. What is fast-track corporate insolvency resolution process. Who can  
undergo fast-track insolvency resolution process as per the provisions of the IBC, 2016?  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The provisions related to the Fast Track Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process is  
provided under Chapter IV Part II of the IBC. It is a specialized framework introduced  
under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code to expedite the resolution process for  
smaller companies with simpler financial structures. It is designed to streamline the  
18  
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes  
insolvency proceedings for eligible corporate debtors, enabling a faster resolution while  
maintaining creditor interests.  
The Fast Track Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process may be made in respect of  
the following corporate debtor as per section 55 of IBC and as notified by the Central  
Government:  
 A small company; or  
 A startup (other than partnership firm); or  
 An unlisted company with total assets, as reported in the financial statement of  
the immediately preceding financial year, not exceeding rupees one crore.  
As per section 56 of the IBC the Fast Track CIRP provides for an accelerated timeline  
for resolution, with a maximum period of 90 days, compared to 180 days in the regular  
CIRP, which can be extended by up to 45 days if required. However, the extension cannot  
be granted more than once. Any extension beyond the said period requires approval from  
the committee of creditors and supported by a vote of seventy five percent of the voting  
share. An application for fast-track corporate insolvency resolution process may be  
filed by a creditor or corporate debtor, as the case may be, along with:  
 the proof of the existence of default as evidenced by records available with an  
information utility or such other means as may be specified by the Board; and  
 such other information as may be specified by the Board to establish that the  
corporate debtor is eligible for fast-track corporate insolvency resolution process.  
Manner of initiating fast track corporate insolvency resolution process.  
Further, as per section 58 of the IBC the process for conducting a corporate  
insolvency resolution process under Chapter II and the provisions relating to offences  
and penalties under Chapter VII shall apply to fast-track corporate insolvency  
resolution process too.  
Thus, the Fast Track Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process offers an expedited  
resolution mechanism for smaller corporate debtors. It aims to reduce timelines while  
maintaining creditor interests and follows a streamlined procedure to achieve a faster  
resolution under the IBC framework.

Question no. 15. What is the objective of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016?  
Explain.  
Ans.  
.
Introduction:  
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (“IBC”) was enacted in India with a set of  
comprehensive objectives aimed at addressing and resolving the complex issues  
related to insolvency, bankruptcy, and financial distress. The IBC consolidates and  
amends the laws relating to reorganization and insolvency resolution of corporate persons,  
partnership firms and individuals in a time bound manner for maximization of value of  
assets of such persons, to promote entrepreneurship, availability of credit and balance the  
interests of all the stakeholders.  
The IBC has some of the key objectives as under:  
 Time-bound Resolution: One of the primary objectives of the IBC is to establish  
a time-bound framework for resolving insolvency cases. It aims to streamline and  
expedite the insolvency resolution process to prevent delays and maximize the  
value of assets.  
 Maximizing Value of Assets: It seeks to maximize the value of distressed assets  
and promote efficient use of resources by facilitating the timely resolution of  
insolvency cases.  
 Protection of the Creditors Interest: It underlines the protection of creditor  
interests by providing them a structured process to recover their dues.  
 Promoting Business as a going concern: It aims to promote business continuity  
and preserve the going concern value of the corporate debtor. The focus is on  
reviving the viable businesses through resolution and restructuring rather than  
liquidation.  
 Institutional Framework: It establishes a well-defined institutional framework for  
insolvency resolution, which includes the National Company Law Tribunal and the  
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India. These institutions ensure effective  
oversight, regulation, and implementation of the insolvency process.  
 Promoting Cross-border Insolvency: Further, the IBC is as per the international  
best practices as it introduces provisions for cross-border insolvency, facilitating  
cooperation between Indian and foreign jurisdictions in insolvency matters.  
Thus, the IBC strives to create a vigorous, time-bound, and effective insolvency  
resolution framework that balances the interests of all stakeholders. It has  
revolutionized the insolvency and bankruptcy laws in India by providing a more  
efficient system for resolving insolvency and bankruptcy cases, leading to faster recovery  
of dues for creditors and a more transparent process for resolving insolvency.  
20  
IBC-Descriptive Question Notes
